chief_complaint: turtle sign retraction of fetal head against perineum immediately after delivery of head in macrosomic infant
hpi_details: 32F G3P2 in second stage of labor delivering a 4.5 kg infant where fetal head delivers but immediately retracts tightly against maternal perineum (turtle sign) with failure of anterior shoulder delivery requiring immediate ALARMER / McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure.
ideas: She thinks the baby is too large and got wedged against her pelvic bone because she stopped pushing properly.
concerns: She is terrified that her baby is being starved of oxygen and will suffer permanent brain damage.
expectations: She hopes the doctor can urgently maneuver and free the baby safely without breaking any bones.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Shoulder dystocia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Shoulder Dystocia Emergency Delivery Protocol, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed clinically when the fetal head delivers but the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with gentle downward traction and routine maternal effort.
Retraction of the delivered fetal head tightly against the perineum (the turtle sign) is a high-specificity warning of an impacted shoulder.
A 4.5 kg infant is a major risk factor, but the emergency is unpredictable and requires immediate action rather than further diagnostic testing.

Record the time of head delivery, fetal status, maneuvers used, and personnel present; after birth, examine the neonate for brachial plexus injury or fracture and the mother for laceration or hemorrhage.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Shoulder dystocia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Macrosomia without dystocia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Turtle sign.
management_principles: Immediately announce shoulder dystocia, call obstetric, anesthesia, and neonatal help, and start timing; do not apply fundal pressure or excessive traction on the fetal head.
First-line maneuvers are McRoberts positioning with suprapubic pressure directed to dislodge the anterior shoulder.
If unresolved, proceed rapidly through trained internal maneuvers (for example Rubin or Woods rotational maneuvers), delivery of the posterior arm, and all-fours positioning as appropriate.
After delivery, assess and document neonatal and maternal injuries, debrief the patient, and discuss recurrence risk in future pregnancies.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Shoulder Dystocia Emergency Delivery Protocol: turtle sign retraction of fetal head against perineum immediately after delivery of head in macrosomic infant. 32F G3P2 in second stage of labor delivering a 4.5 kg infant where fetal head delivers but immediately retracts tightly against maternal perineum (turtle sign) with failure of anterior shoulder delivery requiring immediate ALARMER / McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Shoulder Dystocia Emergency Delivery Protocol.
reference_soap.assessment: Shoulder dystocia with turtle sign during vaginal delivery of a macrosomic infant.
reference_soap.plan: Call for immediate obstetric and neonatal assistance, announce the dystocia, and document head-to-body delivery time. Avoid fundal pressure and excessive traction. Perform McRoberts positioning with suprapubic pressure, then progress promptly to internal rotational maneuvers, delivery of the posterior arm, or all-fours positioning if unresolved. After delivery, assess the neonate for brachial plexus injury/fracture and the mother for postpartum hemorrhage and lacerations.

teaching.one_liner: 32F G3P2 delivering a 4.5kg infant with turtle sign and failure of anterior shoulder delivery.
red_flags: Failure of shoulder delivery after gentle traction

must_ask.objective: Explain what is happening in real time
must_ask.say: The baby's head has delivered but the shoulder is stuck — I need you to follow my instructions closely now.
I need you to bring your knees up tightly to your chest right now.
My assistant will now push firmly just above your pubic bone to help free the shoulder.

must_ask.objective: Instruct the patient not to push
must_ask.say: Please stop pushing for a moment and just breathe with me.
Did you have gestational diabetes or a large baby in a previous pregnancy?

history.answer: The baby's head just delivered, but it immediately pulled right back tightly against her body and the rest of the baby will not come out!
She is at 39 weeks and 4 days today, and she attended all of her scheduled prenatal appointments without missing any.
Her labor pains started naturally at home about eight hours ago without any falls, accidents, or heavy lifting.
She only had a small pinkish mucous show when labor began, with no heavy red bleeding or large blood clots.
Her contractions have been coming every two to three minutes and last about a minute each, and her belly relaxes in between them.
Her water broke about four hours ago in the labor room, and the fluid was completely clear with no foul smell.
The baby was kicking and moving around actively right up until she started pushing in this second stage of labor.
No, she has not had any severe headaches, blurry vision, spots in her eyes, upper right belly pain, or sudden swelling.
She is exhausted and breathing heavily from the hard pushing, but she has not felt dizzy, faint, or noticed a racing heart.
She has had no fever, chills, sweating, or bad-smelling fluid during the entire labor.
Her last scan two weeks ago showed a single baby estimated to be quite large, around 4.4 kilograms, with normal fluid and placenta.
Her blood pressure ran slightly high, but her urine was negative for protein, her blood type is O positive, and her sugar screen was borderline.
She gained about 18 kilograms over the pregnancy, but she has not had extreme thirst or excessive urination beyond what is normal.
This is her third baby; her first two were normal vaginal births weighing 3.6 and 3.9 kilograms with no complications.
We understand that the baby's shoulder is wedged behind her pelvic bone, and we are ready to follow whatever you tell us to do.
I am helping pull her legs and thighs back tightly toward her chest right now to open her pelvis up.
We understand that the nurse is going to push firmly right above her pubic bone to guide the baby's shoulder through.
I am telling her right now to stop pushing and just blow and pant so you can work on freeing the baby.
We know the baby being over four kilograms was a big risk factor, and we want to know what to watch out for once the baby delivers.
I think the baby is just too chubby and got stuck on my pelvic bone when I stopped pushing.
I'm terrified my baby is running out of air in there and is going to suffer brain damage.
She has had chronic high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol for several years, but no other chronic illnesses.
She has never had any surgeries or hospital stays other than the normal deliveries of our first two children.
She takes labetalol 100 milligrams twice a day for her blood pressure and takes a prenatal multivitamin every morning.
She has no known allergies to any medications, latex, or foods.
She has never smoked cigarettes, used cigars, or used electronic nicotine vapes.
She does not drink any alcohol at all and has completely avoided alcohol during the pregnancy.
She works as a middle school teacher and lives in an apartment with me and our two young children.
Her mother has high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, but there are no inherited genetic disorders in the family.
Her last menstrual period started about nine months ago, right near the end of December, with regular monthly cycles before that.
We were not using birth control because this pregnancy was planned, and she had no prior miscarriages.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 136/86 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air.
Diaphoretic, anxious woman in active second stage labor lying in dorsal lithotomy position, actively breathing through contractions.
Distended gravid abdomen consistent with full-term pregnancy; no surgical scars or abnormal surface distension.
Uterus firm with regular contractions occurring every two to three minutes; no uterine tetany or localized tenderness between contractions.
Fetal heart sounds heard in the lower quadrant at 135 beats per minute with reassuring baseline variability.

Fetal head has delivered but is retracted tightly against the maternal perineum with classic turtle sign, and gentle downward traction fails to release the anterior shoulder from behind the pubic bone.
Maternal perineum is stretched taut around the tightly retracted fetal head, with minimal active bleeding and no deep perineal lacerations visible yet.
Trace symmetrical pretibial edema bilaterally, consistent with late pregnancy.
Patellar deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally with no sustained ankle clonus.
